newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Complaints, vodka pour forth on Russian May Day.
newsitem.headline: Complaints, vodka pour forth on Russian May Day.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Russians marched on Thursday to mark the May Day holiday, pouring forth complaints about economic hardship as well as ample amounts of celebratory vodka.
Outside the Kremlin walls, police estimated about 25,000 communist supporters carrying red flags and slogans demanding President Boris Yeltsin's removal.
"All workers should say 'Boris, go away,'" said Viktor Anpilov, head of the hardline communist Working Russia movement.

Later the crowd, estimated at 100,000 by organisers, approved a resolution "demanding the firing of President Yeltsin who has committed monstrous crimes against the country and the people which is inexcusable".
The resolution also condemned plans by NATO to invite new members from eastern Europe to join the Western alliance.
But communist officials apparently decided to call off plans to start gathering signatures demanding Yeltsin's resignation.

At a tamer union-sponsored march of a few thousand people outside Moscow's City Hall, the mood was more festive. Musicians and dancers in traditional dress performed under hazy sun on one of the first warm days at the end of the long Russian winter.
Viktor Rubin, 51, watched the morning entertainment with a friend, carrying a plastic bag with a nearly empty bottle of vodka and plastic cups.
"I'm a blazing communist and he's a democrat and we are drinking together," he said with a broad smile.
Maria, 74, who declined to give her last name, said she had enjoyed decades of May Day celebrations, but was in a sombre mood on Thursday.

"It is a day without happiness for us because our lives have worsened," she said, walking about with her husband. "They've lowered our pensions to only 300,000 roubles ($53) a month. We can't even afford to buy an ice cream and it's a holiday."

Police presence was heavy across the capital to control a repeat of violence that marred the workers' holiday in 1993 when one person was killed and scores were injured in clashes between protesters and riot police.
Red Square, the traditional Mecca of workers on May 1 during Soviet times, was closed to the public and became a staging ground for police reinforcements.

Communist supporters and unions also marched in 900 cities across Russia, police said. In St. Petersburg more than 40,000 people gathered outside the Hermitage. But an overwhelming majority of Russians used the holiday to visit the countryside or relax with friends.

In a pre-recorded radio address, Yeltsin said many people would use the four-day holiday to rest and work at their garden plots. "Others, out of habit, will go to rallies with flags and slogans. They will condemn the authorities, condemn the president," Yeltsin said.
"They have the right to do so and this is what we have fought for. For the citizens' right to decide themselves what they want to do, both on working days and on holidays."
Some communists tried at least for a moment to pretend the Soviet Union was alive and well, the old May Day thriving.
"I love, you, dear Russia, happy holiday to the Soviet Union!" one elderly woman told the Moscow communist rally, promting a rousing "Hurrah!" from the masses.

But in the southern Russian city of Pyatigorsk, where a bomb at the local train station killed two people on Monday, officials called off public celebrations after an anonymous telephone threat, Itar-Tass news agency reported.
